usage: 나다 = the illness 'came out'; never use 받다 or 가지다 here
심하다, not 크다, describes how severe a condition is
고치다 is the casual verb for fixing illness or objects alike
걸리다 needs 에; this fixed phrase = 'got hooked by' a disease
examples: 저는 병이 안 나서 다행이에요.
I'm relieved I didn't get sick.
Simple: 병이 나다 ('fall ill'), negated as 안 나다; the most basic frame.
할아버지가 큰 병에 걸려서 입원하셨어요.
Grandpa caught a serious disease, so he was hospitalized.
Everyday: 큰 병 collocates with 걸리다 + 에, and 입원하다 = be admitted.
이 병은 약으로 못 고치고 수술을 받아야 해요.
This disease can't be cured with medicine; you have to get surgery.
Real-situation: contrasts 고치다(cure) with 수술을 받다(undergo surgery).
nuance: 병 is the Sino-Korean word 病, the broad term for any illness from a cold to cancer; for a serious one Koreans add 큰 (큰 병) and for a minor one they often switch to 감기 or 몸살 instead. Two patterns split by particle: 병이 나다 (a disease 'breaks out,' using 나다 like 열이 나다 'run a fever') versus 병에 걸리다 ('get hooked by' a disease, requiring 에 exactly as 감기에 걸리다). The big English-speaker trap is forcing 'catch' into 받다 or 가지다 — Korean treats catching a disease as being snagged by it, so 병을 걸리다 (wrong particle) and 병을 받다 both sound broken; the disease is the thing you bump into, marked with 에. 병 is neutral in register and fine in both polite and casual speech, but when speaking about an elder's illness you raise the verb politely (병에 걸리셨어요).

mistakes: Saying 병을 걸렸어요: 걸리다 demands the location/contact particle 에, so it must be 병에 걸렸어요.
Saying 병을 받았어요 by translating 'I caught a disease' literally: 받다 is for handing-over; use 병에 걸렸어요 or 병이 났어요.
Treating 병 like a countable thing you 'have' as in 병을 가지고 있어요: Koreans say 병이 있어요 (state of having an illness), not 가지다.

usage: 맞다 (lit. 'be struck') is how the patient RECEIVES the injection
아프다 describes the painful sensation of the shot itself
놓다 is the action of the person ADMINISTERING it
무섭다 marks the feared thing with 가, not 를
examples: 저는 주사를 맞기 싫어요.
I don't want to get a shot.
Simple: patient's side always pairs 주사 with 맞다.
감기가 심해서 병원에서 주사를 맞았어요.
My cold was bad, so I got a shot at the clinic.
Everyday: 주사 맞다 is the standard clinic experience after a 감기.
간호사 선생님이 아이 팔에 주사를 놓아 주셨어요.
The nurse gave the child a shot in the arm.
Real-situation: the giver uses 놓다, and -아 주시다 adds politeness for the nurse.
nuance: 주사 is Sino-Korean 注射, literally 'pour (注) and shoot (射),' a vivid image of forcing fluid in through a needle. The crucial point is that the verb flips depending on who acts: the patient says 주사를 맞다 — and 맞다 literally means 'to be hit/struck,' the same verb as in 비를 맞다 (get rained on) or 매를 맞다 (get beaten), framing the shot as something done TO you — while the nurse who administers it says 주사를 놓다 ('lay/place' the shot). English speakers almost always reach for 받다 ('receive') because 'receive a shot' feels logical, but 주사를 받다 sounds unnatural; 받다 is reserved for treatment as a whole (치료를 받다), not the needle. Note 주사 covers the whole injection event, while the physical needle is 주삿바늘 and the syringe is 주사기.

mistakes: Saying 주사를 받아요: the patient-side verb is 맞다, so it must be 주사를 맞아요; 받다 collocates with 치료, not 주사.
Using 놓다 for yourself as the patient (주사를 놓았어요 meaning 'I got a shot'): 놓다 is the giver's verb; the patient says 맞았어요.
Saying 주사가 무서워해요 to mean 'I'm scared of shots': 무서워하다 needs a human subject; for the shot itself use 주사가 무서워요.

usage: 받다 = the patient RECEIVES the course of care
끝나다 (intransitive) means the process finished on its own
필요하다 marks what is needed with 가, not 를
시작하다 takes 를 for what you start
examples: 빨리 치료를 받으세요.
Please get treatment quickly.
Simple: patient + 치료를 받다, the core medical-care frame.
3주 동안 병원에서 치료를 받고 많이 좋아졌어요.
I got treatment at the hospital for three weeks and improved a lot.
Everyday: 동안 (duration) + 치료를 받다 + 좋아지다 (get better).
의사 선생님이 환자를 정성껏 치료해 주셨어요.
The doctor treated the patient with great care.
Real-situation: the doctor's side uses the verb 치료하다, not 받다.
nuance: 치료 is Sino-Korean 治療, where 治 means 'to govern/manage' and 療 means 'to heal,' together 'managing an illness back to health' — broader than a single procedure, it covers the whole healing process (medication, therapy, surgery as a package). Watch the actor split exactly as with 주사: the patient says 치료를 받다 ('receive treatment'), while the doctor says 환자를 치료하다 ('treat the patient'), so 받다 vs the 하다-verb tells you who is acting. The nearest neighbor is 진료 (診療, 'examine + heal'), which is narrower — 진료 is the consultation/seeing-the-doctor part (진료를 받다 = 'see a doctor'), whereas 치료 is the actual curing that follows. English speakers sometimes carry over the 'shot' verb and say 치료를 맞다; that is wrong — 맞다 belongs only to 주사. They also drop the particle in 치료가 필요하다, mistakenly saying 치료를 필요해요.

usage: 많다 takes 가 for what is plentiful
보다 = a doctor examining; never 만나다 here
I take care of a patient
돌보다 = look after, nurse a patient
회복하다 (回復) for getting well again
examples: 오늘은 환자가 별로 없어요.
There aren't many patients today.
Simple: 환자가 + existence/quantity verb, the most basic frame.
응급실에 환자가 많아서 한참 기다렸어요.
There were many patients in the ER, so I waited a long time.
Everyday: 환자가 많다 + 기다리다 in a real hospital scene.
의사 선생님이 입원 환자들을 한 명씩 봐요.
The doctor sees the inpatients one by one.
Real-situation: 환자를 보다 (examine) + 입원 환자 (inpatient) + 한 명씩.
nuance: 환자 is Sino-Korean 患者, literally 患 'to suffer/afflict' + 者 'person,' i.e. 'a suffering person' — note that 者 is the same 'person' suffix in 기자(reporter) and 과학자(scientist), so the word is built on the idea of one afflicted by illness. The biggest pitfall is the verb for a doctor's exam: Korean says 환자를 보다, using 보다 ('look at') the way a doctor 'looks over' a case, NOT 만나다 ('meet'); 환자를 만나다 sounds like a casual social encounter, not a medical visit, so a doctor never says it about examining someone. Register-wise 환자 is a neutral clinical noun; when the patient is an elder you may add honorifics elsewhere in the sentence (보호자/분), but 환자 itself stays plain. A near term is 손님 — a pharmacy or clinic might call walk-ins 손님 (customers), but inside a hospital the sick person is specifically 환자.

mistakes: Saying 의사가 환자를 만나요 to mean a doctor examines a patient: that sounds like a social meet-up; use 환자를 봐요.

Adding wrong honorific verbs to 환자 reflexively (환자께서): 환자 is a neutral noun; honorifics attach by context, not automatically.

usage: 재다 = measure, the same verb as for height/length
높다 (high), not 크다 (big), for a reading
정상 (正常) = normal; ~이에요 after a consonant
examples: 체온계로 체온을 재요.
I take the temperature with a thermometer.
Simple: instrument 체온계 + 체온을 재다, the core measuring frame.
열이 나서 체온을 재 보니 38도였어요.
I had a fever, so I checked and my temperature was 38 degrees.
Everyday: 재 보다 (try measuring) + ~도 for degrees Celsius.
아기 체온이 갑자기 올라가서 병원에 데려갔어요.
The baby's temperature suddenly went up, so I took them to the hospital.
Real-situation: 체온이 올라가다 (rises) + 데려가다 (take a person).
nuance: 체온 is Sino-Korean 體溫, literally 體 'body' + 溫 'warmth,' so it specifically means the warmth of the body, distinct from 온도 (溫度, 'temperature-degree'), which is the general word for any temperature — air, water, an oven. Use 체온 only for a person or animal's heat and 온도 for the room or weather; saying 방 체온 (room body-temperature) is wrong, it must be 방 온도. The verb is 재다 ('to measure'), the very same verb used for 키를 재다 (measure height) and 길이를 재다 (measure length), because temperature is a quantity you gauge, not something you 'look at' — so 체온을 보다 sounds off to natives. For a high or low reading Korean uses 높다/낮다, never 크다/작다 (big/small), which is the typical English-speaker slip. A closely related symptom word is 열 (fever): 열이 나다 means 'run a fever,' and you confirm it by 체온을 재다.

Saying 체온을 봐요 instead of 재요: temperature is measured with an instrument, so the verb is 재다.

usage: 재다 = measure, same verb as 체온/키
높다, never 크다, for the reading
낮다 = low; common cause of dizziness
examples: 집에서 매일 혈압을 재요.
I take my blood pressure at home every day.
Simple: habit + 혈압을 재다, the core measuring frame.
우리 아버지는 혈압이 높아서 약을 드세요.
My father has high blood pressure, so he takes medicine.
Everyday: 혈압이 높다 + 약을 드시다 (honorific 'take medicine').
갑자기 일어나면 혈압이 떨어져서 어지러울 수 있어요.
If you stand up suddenly, your blood pressure can drop and you may feel dizzy.
Real-situation: 혈압이 떨어지다 (drops) + 어지럽다 (dizzy) + ~을 수 있다.
nuance: 혈압 is Sino-Korean 血壓, literally 血 'blood' + 壓 'pressure,' a transparent compound naming the pressure of blood in the vessels. Like 체온, it is something you gauge, so the verb is 재다 ('measure') — the identical verb in 키를 재다 and 체온을 재다 — and high/low readings take 높다/낮다, the persistent English-speaker error being 크다/작다 (big/small), which are for physical size, not measured values. For movement of the reading, Korean uses 오르다/올라가다 (rises) and 떨어지다/내려가다 (drops), not 'go up/down' translated as 가다. Distinguish 혈압 from 맥박 (脈搏, pulse/heart rate): both are vital signs taken at the clinic, but 혈압 is the pressure number and 맥박 is the beats per minute. In casual talk people with chronic hypertension say 고혈압 (高血壓, 'high blood pressure' as a named condition), so 고혈압이 있어요 means 'I have hypertension,' a step beyond a one-time high reading.

usage: 아프다 for the pain of the cut
examples: 손가락에 작은 상처가 났어요.
I got a small cut on my finger.
Simple: body part + 에 + 상처가 나다, the core 'get hurt' frame.
넘어져서 무릎에 상처가 났는데 피가 났어요.
I fell and got a wound on my knee, and it bled.
Everyday: 넘어지다(fall) + 상처가 나다 + 피가 나다 (bleed).
연고를 바르고 며칠 지나니까 상처가 깨끗이 나았어요.
I applied ointment, and after a few days the wound healed cleanly.
Real-situation: 연고를 바르다(apply ointment) + 낫다 for healing.
nuance: 상처 is Sino-Korean 傷處, literally 傷 'injure/wound' + 處 'place/spot,' i.e. 'the injured spot' on the body. Crucially, 상처 has a famous double life: physically it is a cut or wound (상처가 나다), but emotionally it means a hurt feeling, and there the collocation flips to 상처를 받다 ('receive a wound,' = be hurt) or 상처를 주다 ('give a wound,' = hurt someone). So a physical injury uses 나다 (it 'comes out'), while an emotional one uses 받다/주다 — mixing these is the classic trap: 상처를 받았어요 about a knee scrape sounds like your feelings were hurt, not your skin. For healing, use 낫다, an ㅅ-irregular verb that drops the ㅅ before a vowel (낫다 → 나아요, 나았어요), and it doubles as 'recover from illness' (감기가 나았어요). A near-synonym is 흉터 (scar) — 상처 is the fresh open wound, 흉터 is the lasting mark it leaves after it heals.

Conjugating 낫다 regularly as 낫아요: it is ㅅ-irregular, so the wound healed = 상처가 나았어요 (나아요).

usage: 하다 = perform the act of coughing
심하다 for a severe, persistent cough
examples: 목이 간지러워서 기침이 나요.
My throat is itchy, so I keep coughing.
Simple: cause 목이 간지럽다 + 기침이 나다, the involuntary frame.
회의 중에 자꾸 기침을 해서 미안했어요.
I kept coughing during the meeting, so I felt sorry.
Everyday: 기침을 하다 (active) + 자꾸 (repeatedly) in a social setting.
기침이 2주 넘게 안 멈추면 병원에 가 보세요.
If a cough doesn't stop for over two weeks, go see a doctor.
Real-situation: 안 멈추다 + 가 보다 (go and see), giving health advice.
nuance: 기침 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean), and it works in two equally natural patterns that differ subtly in viewpoint: 기침이 나다 frames the cough as something that 'comes out' on its own — built with 나다, the same verb in 열이 나다(run a fever), 콧물이 나다(runny nose), 재채기가 나다(sneeze) — stressing it's involuntary; whereas 기침을 하다 frames it as an action you perform, useful when you mean someone coughs deliberately or repeatedly. English speakers raised on 'have a cough' often try 기침을 가지다 ('possess a cough'), which is flatly wrong — Korean never 'has' a symptom with 가지다; symptoms either 나다 (come out) or you 하다 (do) them. Don't confuse 기침 with 재채기 (a sneeze): 기침 is a throat/chest cough, 재채기 is the explosive nose sneeze, and they are not interchangeable. For severity use 심하다 (기침이 심하다 = a bad cough), not 크다.

English speakers raised on 'have a cough' often try 기침을 가지다 ('possess a cough'), which is flatly wrong — Korean never 'has' a symptom with 가지다; symptoms either 나다 (come out) or you 하다 (do) them.

mistakes: Saying 기침을 가지고 있어요 from English 'I have a cough': symptoms use 나다 or 하다, so say 기침이 나요 / 기침을 해요.
Confusing 기침 with 재채기: a throat cough is 기침; the nose sneeze is 재채기.
Saying 기침이 커요 for a bad cough: severity is 심하다, so it must be 기침이 심해요.

usage: 많다 for a heavy runny nose
닦다 = wipe away with a tissue
examples: 날씨가 추워서 콧물이 나요.
It's cold out, so my nose is running.
Simple: cause 춥다 + 콧물이 나다, the core symptom frame.
감기에 걸려서 콧물하고 기침이 같이 나요.
I caught a cold, so I have a runny nose and a cough together.
Everyday: 콧물 + 기침 both with 나다, listed via 하고.
휴지로 콧물을 닦고 손을 깨끗이 씻으세요.
Wipe your nose with a tissue and wash your hands well.
Real-situation: 콧물을 닦다 (active wipe) + hygiene advice.
nuance: 콧물 is a native compound: 코 (nose) + the linking ㅅ (사이시옷) + 물 (water), literally 'nose-water' — that inserted ㅅ is why it's spelled 콧물 and pronounced [콘물], a tiny spelling point learners miss. Like other discharges it pairs with 나다 (콧물이 나다, 'snot comes out'), exactly parallel to 눈물이 나다 (tears) and 땀이 나다 (sweat), so the whole family of bodily fluids shares this 나다 frame. The key English-speaker trap is reaching for 코가 아프다 ('my nose hurts') to express a cold — but that means literal nose pain, not a runny nose; a stuffy/congested nose is yet another phrase, 코가 막히다 ('the nose is blocked'). So three different states: 콧물이 나다 (runny), 코가 막히다 (stuffy), 코가 아프다 (painful). When you actively clear it you 닦다 (wipe) or 풀다 (blow: 코를 풀다). Register is fully neutral and used freely in everyday talk and at the clinic.

mistakes: Saying 코가 아파요 to mean a runny nose: that's literal nose pain; a runny nose is 콧물이 나요.
Saying 콧물이 막혔어요 mixing up symptoms: a blocked nose is 코가 막혔어요; running is 콧물이 나요.
Misspelling as 코물 without the 사이시옷: it must be 콧물 (pronounced [콘물]).

usage: 두통약 = headache pill; 약을 먹다 idiom
examples: 어제부터 두통이 있어요.
I've had a headache since yesterday.
Simple: ~부터 (since) + 두통이 있다, the core 'have a headache' frame.
스트레스 때문에 두통이 심해서 일찍 퇴근했어요.
My headache was bad from stress, so I left work early.
Everyday: 때문에(because) + 두통이 심하다 + 퇴근하다 (leave work).
두통약을 먹고 한숨 자고 나니까 좀 괜찮아졌어요.
I took a headache pill, slept a bit, and felt somewhat better.
Real-situation: 두통약을 먹다 + 자고 나다 + 괜찮아지다 (get better).
nuance: 두통 is Sino-Korean 頭痛, literally 頭 'head' + 痛 'ache/pain' — the same 痛 appears in 복통 (腹痛, stomachache) and 치통 (齒痛, toothache), so once you know 통 = 'ache' the whole pain family opens up. The register split matters: 두통 is the bookish/clinical word you'd write on a pharmacy form or say to a doctor, while in everyday speech Koreans far more often say 머리가 아파요 ('my head hurts') with the native adjective 아프다. Both are correct, but to a friend 머리 아파 sounds natural and 두통이 있어 sounds slightly formal. The number-one English-speaker error is double-marking the pain: since 두통 already contains 痛 ('ache'), saying 두통이 아파요 literally means 'the headache hurts' — redundant and wrong; the noun takes 있다/심하다, not 아프다. Use 아프다 only with the body part (머리가 아프다), never with 두통.

usage: 안 되다 = it doesn't happen; the standard 'upset stomach'
돕다 (ㅂ-irregular) = help; subject is a food/drink
examples: 저는 우유를 마시면 소화가 잘 안 돼요.
When I drink milk, I don't digest it well.
Simple: condition + 소화가 안 되다, the core indigestion frame.
급하게 먹으면 소화가 안 되니까 천천히 드세요.
If you eat in a hurry you'll get indigestion, so please eat slowly.
Everyday: 급하게(hastily) + 소화가 안 되다 + advice with 드세요.
체했을 때는 소화제를 먹거나 손을 따 주면 좋아요.
When your stomach is upset, taking a digestive or pricking the finger helps.
Real-situation: 체하다 (have indigestion) + 소화제 + folk remedy.
nuance: 소화 is Sino-Korean 消化, literally 消 'dissolve/dissipate' + 化 'transform' — food being broken down and changed inside you. The governing verb is 되다 ('to become/happen'), so 소화가 되다 = 'digestion takes place' and 소화가 안 되다 = 'indigestion,' the everyday way to say your stomach is off. The big trap for English speakers is treating digestion as an action you do: 소화를 하다 or 소화를 못 하다 sounds unnatural, because Korean frames digestion as something that happens to/in you (되다), not something you actively perform — so 'I can't digest' is 소화가 안 돼요, never 소화를 못 해요. A close real-life synonym is the native verb 체하다, which is more acute: 소화가 안 되다 is general slow/poor digestion, while 체하다 means you got an actual blockage/upset stomach from eating, often suddenly. The medicine is 소화제 (消化劑, 'digestion-agent'), built with the same 劑 as 해열제 (fever reducer).

mistakes: Saying 소화를 못 해요 for 'I can't digest': digestion is framed with 되다, so say 소화가 안 돼요.
Saying 소화를 해요 to mean 'I digest': it must be the happening-verb 소화가 잘 돼요, not 소화를 하다.
Treating 소화가 안 되다 and 체하다 as identical: 체하다 is a sudden upset stomach from eating; 소화가 안 되다 is general poor digestion.

usage: 좋다, not 높다, describes good health
챙기다 = take care of, mind one's health
examples: 건강이 제일 중요해요.
Health is the most important thing.
Simple: 건강이 + adjective, the core 'health is X' frame.
요즘 운동을 시작해서 건강이 많이 좋아졌어요.
I started exercising lately, so my health has improved a lot.
Everyday: 운동을 시작하다 + 건강이 좋아지다 (improve).
할머니, 늘 건강하시고 오래오래 사세요.
Grandma, please always stay healthy and live a long, long life.
Real-situation: honorific 건강하시다 + 사세요 as a warm blessing.
nuance: 건강 is Sino-Korean 健康, where 健 means 'sturdy/robust' and 康 means 'peaceful/well,' together the sound, robust state of body and mind. It splits into a noun and an adjective: the noun 건강 ('health') pairs with 좋다/나쁘다 (good/bad) — never 높다/낮다 (high/low), which is the typical English-influenced slip from 'high level of health' — and you actively mind it with 챙기다 (건강을 챙기다, 'look after your health'); the adjective 건강하다 means 'to be healthy' (저는 건강해요 = 'I'm healthy'). Its honorific imperative 건강하세요 is a beloved set phrase, a warm farewell/blessing meaning 'stay healthy,' especially said to elders and at New Year. A near-synonym is 컨디션 (a loanword from 'condition') — but 컨디션 is your day-to-day fitness/energy level (오늘 컨디션이 안 좋아 = 'I'm not feeling great today'), whereas 건강 is your overall, long-term state of wellness; don't swap them.

It splits into a noun and an adjective: the noun 건강 ('health') pairs with 좋다/나쁘다 (good/bad) and you actively mind it with 챙기다 (건강을 챙기다, 'look after your health'); the adjective 건강하다 means 'to be healthy' (저는 건강해요 = 'I'm healthy').
